summary.text: A nonzero determinant forces at least one matrix entry to be nonzero; the two primes encoded by that entry sum to \(2n\), since the opposite index shifts cancel. Taking \(n=2k+1\) handles \(k\ge 60\), while the finitely many cases \(1\le k\le 59\) are settled by explicit prime decompositions.

full_proof.text:
Let \(n\ge 1\), and let \(M_n\) be the \(n\times n\) matrix defining \(a(n)=A228623(n)\). Its rows and columns are indexed by integers \(i,j\) with \(0\le i,j<n\), and
\[
(M_n)_{ij}=
\begin{cases}
1,&\text{if both }n+i-j\text{ and }n+j-i\text{ are prime},\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Here the expressions are natural-number differences. They agree with the usual integer differences: since \(j<n\), we have \(j\le n+i\), and since \(i<n\), we have \(i\le n+j\). In particular, for every pair of indices,
\[
(n+i-j)+(n+j-i)=2n. \tag{1}
\]

We first establish the key consequence of a nonzero determinant.

**Lemma.** If \(n>0\) and \(a(n)\ne 0\), then there are primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
p+q=2n.
\]

Indeed, suppose, to the contrary, that no two primes sum to \(2n\). Consider any entry of \(M_n\), with indices \(i,j\). If that entry were \(1\), then
\[
p=n+i-j,\qquad q=n+j-i
\]
would both be prime. Equation (1) would then give \(p+q=2n\), contrary to the supposition. Hence every entry of \(M_n\) is zero, so \(M_n\) is the zero matrix. Since \(n>0\), its determinant is zero: for example, in the permutation expansion of its determinant, every product contains a zero matrix entry. Thus \(a(n)=\det(M_n)=0\), contradicting \(a(n)\ne0\). This proves the lemma.

Now assume the conjectured nonvanishing statement:
\[
\text{for every odd integer }n>120,\qquad a(n)\ne0. \tag{2}
\]
We prove that every integer \(4k+2\) with \(k>0\) is a sum of two primes.

Fix a positive integer \(k\). We divide into two cases.

### Case 1: \(k\ge 60\)

Set
\[
n=2k+1.
\]
This number is odd. Moreover,
\[
n=2k+1\ge 2\cdot60+1=121>120.
\]
Consequently, (2) gives \(a(n)\ne0\). Also \(n>0\), so the lemma supplies primes \(p,q\) satisfying
\[
p+q=2n.
\]
Substituting \(n=2k+1\), we obtain
\[
p+q=2(2k+1)=4k+2,
\]
which is the desired prime decomposition.

### Case 2: \(k<60\)

Since \(k>0\), this means \(1\le k\le59\). The required decompositions are given explicitly in the following table. An entry \(k:p+q\) means that \(4k+2=p+q\).

\[
\begin{array}{c|c@{\qquad}c|c@{\qquad}c|c}
k&p+q&k&p+q&k&p+q\\ \hline
1&3+3&2&3+7&3&3+11\\
4&5+13&5&3+19&6&3+23\\
7&7+23&8&3+31&9&7+31\\
10&5+37&11&3+43&12&3+47\\
13&7+47&14&5+53&15&3+59\\
16&5+61&17&3+67&18&3+71\\
19&5+73&20&3+79&21&3+83\\
22&7+83&23&5+89&24&19+79\\
25&5+97&26&3+103&27&3+107\\
28&5+109&29&5+113&30&13+109\\
31&13+113&32&3+127&33&3+131\\
34&7+131&35&3+139&36&7+139\\
37&11+139&38&3+151&39&7+151\\
40&5+157&41&3+163&42&3+167\\
43&7+167&44&5+173&45&3+179\\
46&5+181&47&11+179&48&3+191\\
49&5+193&50&3+199&51&7+199\\
52&11+199&53&3+211&54&7+211\\
55&11+211&56&3+223&57&3+227\\
58&5+229&59&5+233&&
\end{array}
\]

In every row the displayed sum is directly equal to \(4k+2\). All displayed summands are prime. For completeness, the only primes that occur as possible trial divisors of an integer at most \(233\) are \(2,3,5,7,11,13\), because \(\sqrt{233}<16\). The displayed summands greater than \(13\) are readily checked not to be divisible by any of these six primes; the smaller displayed summands \(3,5,7,11,13\) are themselves prime. Thus the table is a complete finite prime-decomposition check for every \(k\) in the interval \(1\le k\le59\).

The two cases cover every positive integer \(k\). Therefore, under the assumption that \(a(n)\ne0\) for every odd \(n>120\), for every \(k>0\) there exist primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
4k+2=p+q.
\]
This is precisely Goldbach’s assertion for the even integers of the form \(4k+2\).
